details:
**Acadia National Park and Mount Desert Island**
Acadia, the most frequent giveaway for Maine, is a national park on the rocky Atlantic coast. Most of it lies on Mount Desert Island, and it also includes parts of the Schoodic Peninsula and Isle au Haut. Features include Eagle Lake and the glacial erratic boulder called Bubble Rock.

**Augusta**
The capital of Maine, located on the Kennebec River. It appears in nearly every final line, often alongside the state's largest cities, Portland, Bangor, and Lewiston.

**Mount Katahdin and Baxter State Park**
Mount Katahdin is Maine's highest peak and the northern end of the Appalachian Trail. It sits inside Baxter State Park, a large wilderness park in the north-central part of the state. In 1939, twelve-year-old Donn Fendler survived nine days lost on Katahdin, a story later told in the book "Lost on a Mountain in Maine."

**Cadillac Mountain**
The highest point on Mount Desert Island, inside Acadia National Park. It is the tallest mountain along the U.S. Atlantic coast, and at certain times of year it is one of the first places in the country to see the sunrise.

**Moosehead Lake and the Kennebec River**
Moosehead Lake is the largest lake in Maine and the source of the Kennebec River, which flows south through Augusta into the Gulf of Maine. The lake also hosts an annual International Seaplane Fly-In each September.

**Portland and Casco Bay**
Portland is Maine's largest city and main seaport, on Casco Bay, and shares its name with Portland, Oregon. Its Munjoy Hill is home to the Portland Observatory, the last remaining maritime signal tower in the United States.

**Penobscot River, Penobscot Bay, and Bangor**
The Penobscot River flows past the city of Bangor into Penobscot Bay, a center of the state's lobster fishing. Bangor is home to a 31-foot statue of the folk-hero lumberjack Paul Bunyan, and Isle au Haut sits at the entrance to the bay.

**Hundred-Mile Wilderness**
A stretch of the Appalachian Trail in Maine leading toward Katahdin. It is known as the longest and most remote section of the trail without roads or towns, so hikers must carry all their supplies.

**Aroostook County and the Aroostook War**
Aroostook is Maine's large, northernmost county, which includes the cities of Presque Isle and Caribou. It gives its name to the "bloodless" Aroostook War (1838–1839), a border dispute with British Canada that was settled by the Webster–Ashburton Treaty of 1842.

**Quoddy Head and Eastport**
West Quoddy Head, a state park near Lubec, is the easternmost point of the contiguous United States, so it is often called the closest U.S. point to Africa. The nearby city of Eastport claims to be the first in the nation to see the sunrise. The Old Sow whirlpool, the largest tidal whirlpool in the Western Hemisphere, lies off Eastport.

**Campobello Island**
A Canadian island in New Brunswick whose only road link is a bridge from Lubec, Maine. It is famous as the site of Franklin D. Roosevelt's summer home.

**New Hampshire as its only neighbor**
Maine is the only U.S. state that borders exactly one other state, New Hampshire, to its west. Its other land borders are with the Canadian provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick.

**Down East, the Schoodic Peninsula, and Bar Harbor**
"Down East" is the name for Maine's eastern coastal region, which includes towns such as Ellsworth and Calais. The Schoodic Peninsula, the only mainland part of Acadia, lies across Frenchman Bay from the tourist town of Bar Harbor on Mount Desert Island.

**Saint John River and the Republic of Madawaska**
The Saint John River forms part of Maine's northern border with New Brunswick before flowing into the Bay of Fundy. The Republic of Madawaska was an unrecognized "republic" in the disputed borderland along this river.

**Kennebunkport and Walker's Point**
Kennebunkport, a coastal town in southern Maine, is home to Walker's Point, the summer estate of the Bush family, including President George H. W. Bush.
